F2.Q1: Cut stone slabs — pale sandstone or limestone flagging, laid in courses with dark mortar joints.
F2.Q1_WHY: The colour under the lamp (300,180) is `255,192,114` — a warm bone-cream, not the grey of granite or the red of brick. The pieces are rectangular, laid in horizontal courses about 25px deep with widths varying between roughly 25 and 75px (visible across 190–630, 8–255), which is dressed slab, not cobble and not poured. Magnified 6× at 500–630, 20–180 the faces carry short parallel 45° strokes, which read as chisel-dressing. The joints are consistently 2px and darker than the faces, so the pieces are set with something between them rather than butted.
F2.Q2:
South, down the corridor at x 370–445.

I picked it off the **walls, not the ground.** The wall line at y≈265 has exactly one gap in it and the corridor runs from there to the bottom of the frame — that's a layout read, not a surface read. The ground in that gap (372–446, 225–264) is indistinguishable from the ground in the room's dead corners: I measured dark-mark coverage of 0.334 at the doorway against 0.366 to the west (240–314, same row) and 0.282 to the east. The doorway is, if anything, *cleaner* than the corner nobody goes to. Nothing about the floor moved me.
F2.Q3: It has been cracked and it has been spotted, and that is the whole story. A web of thin fractures crosses it, and about fourteen dark rosette-shaped blots are scattered across it. What has *not* happened: nothing is worn, nothing is polished, nothing is chipped, no slab has sunk or lifted or gone missing, no edge is rounded, there is no grit, no dust, no accumulation in the joints, no threshold stone at the doorway. It reads as a floor that has been *damaged* but never *used*.
F2.Q3_WHY: Sampling in the bright zone: slab face (300,180) = `255,192,114`; vertical joint (347,175) = `112,80,52`; crack pixel (303,206) = `92,67,44`; stain core (268,232) = `96,70,48`. **Structure, damage and filth are all rendered at the same value** — within about 20 levels of each other. At 1:1 they collapse into one uniform black web and I cannot tell a joint from a break. Every slab face in that web is the same clean cream. In the corridor (360–450, 265–430) it's the same: one long crack down the centre and otherwise pristine slabs, on a route the fiction says is walked daily. Nobody's feet have touched this.
F2.Q4:
Two things.

First, **the hard diagonal seam in the lighting** running down-left through roughly (330,60) → (200,190), clearest magnified at 190–340, 60–200. It's a stair-stepped edge between two light levels, cutting straight across slab faces and joints alike with no regard for the geometry. At 1:1 it is the single strongest feature on the floor — a light artefact out-reading every piece of art underneath it.

Second, **the rosettes.** Same spiky-ringed silhouette, same ~20px diameter, roughly fourteen of them: (223,38), (237,48), (376,48), (429,22), (300,86), (543,86), (563,86), (405,106), (537,150), (341,166), (217,172), (225,194), (269,230), (543,214). Template-matching one against the others returns a best score of 0.436, so they're genuinely varied rather than one stamp copied — but they are all the *same size* and spread at near-uniform density, about one every three tiles, right across the room including the corners the light barely reaches. They don't cluster under anything, don't trail anywhere, don't thin out. After the third one my eye starts reading them as a scatter setting rather than as marks.
F2.Q5:
**Made** — but made by a process, not by a hand.

I ran an autocorrelation over the lighting-normalised floor (190–625, 10–255) across every offset up to dy=120, dx=200. The best non-trivial score is 0.27 at dx=60 — no periodicity worth the name. The slab layout, the crack routes and the blots are all unique across the room. That's genuinely authored, and it's more than most floors manage.

What gives away the machine is the orientation histogram. Weighted gradient energy over the floor lives at 0–10° (3104), 90–100° (3198), 40–50° (1384) and 130–140° (1462). The bins in between — 20–30°, 60–70°, 110–120°, 150–160° — sit at 221–231, essentially empty. **Every mark on this floor is at 0°, 45° or 90° and nothing else.** Real fracture and real wear spray across every angle. This is a generator drawing with a pixel-perfect brush at four canonical headings.
F2.Q6:
**YES.**

Merely competent. The layout variation is real work and the crack routing is better than placeholder. But it's competent, not good — the faces are empty, the value separation between structure and damage doesn't exist, and the surface carries no information a player could act on.
F2.Q7:
Legible at 1:1 — but all of it is *edges between* pieces, not the face of the material:
- the joint grid
- the crack web (indistinguishable from the joint grid)
- the dark rosette blots
- a soft diagonal shading on the mid-lit slabs

**The faces themselves are blank at 1:1.** In the bright zone the slabs at (280–400, 150–220) are flat unbroken cream. Nothing on them.

Only appears once magnified: the parallel 45° chisel hatch, and stacks of 3–5 short horizontal dashes. I found those at 4× and had to push contrast 2.2× to be sure they were marks rather than dither. **That is hunting, not seeing.** At 1:1 they register as a vague tonal smudge, and in the brightest third of the floor they register as nothing at all, because the red channel is clipped to 255 across 8.2% of the floor in a blob spanning x 289–426, y 87–254 — directly under and around the figure. The lamp is bleaching out the exact area the player is looking at. Measured face variance is 0.136 under the lamp against 0.22–0.26 everywhere else: the light is destroying more detail than the art is supplying.
F2.Q7_WHY: Checked at 1:1 — (440–630, 20–180) mid-lit right side; (260–450, 140–300) bright zone with the figure; (190–380, 0–160) upper left; (360–450, 265–590) corridor. Had to magnify — (500–630, 20–180) at 6× with contrast for the hatch and dashes; (190–340, 60–200) at 5× for the light seam; (180–380, 110–265) at 4× for the rosette edges.
F2.Q8:
It reads as **one age everywhere, and that age is roughly a decade** — a sound floor that has been shaken hard and stained, not an ancient one.

The cracking argues for a lot of time, or one violent event. But everything that only accumulates *slowly* is missing, and its absence is what caps the age. Across the whole lit floor there is no rounding on a single slab edge — every corner in (192–608, 8–255) is a clean 90° pixel corner. No joint has widened or lost its fill; joint width is a uniform 2px from (195,20) to (600,250). No slab is displaced in height, dished, or replaced with a different stone. There is no accumulated grime gradient — dark-mark coverage measures 0.334, 0.366, 0.282, 0.342 across four widely separated regions, i.e. flat, when age produces gradients.

Set against the fiction, this is the wrong reading: a filing system for souls, in continuous heavy use since before the records, ought to have slabs polished into hollows and joints packed solid with centuries of tread. Nothing here is worn. **The corridor at (360–450, 265–430) — a daily route — is the newest-looking ground in the image.**
F2.Q9:
The corridor runs south and the light gives up around y≈430. So yes, I can see where it goes — **but I read it off the walls, not the ground.** The ground told me almost nothing.

The one thing the ground contributes is accidental: a single long crack runs down the corridor's centre line from about (398,280) to (410,590), nearly parallel with the axis of travel. It happens to point the right way. But it's damage, not a path — there's no wear channel, no darkened centre, no clean margin where feet don't fall, no debris pushed to the sides. If that crack had been routed across the corridor instead of along it, my read of the route would be unchanged, which tells you it isn't actually carrying the information.
F2.Q9_WHY: Route regions — (372–446, 225–264) the doorway approach, (368–448, 265–430) the lit corridor. Rejected — (240–314, 225–264) west floor, (500–574, 225–264) east floor, (300–374, 60–110) north-west interior. **What is different about the ground between them: nothing measurable.** Dark-mark coverage 0.334 / 0.395 on the route against 0.366 / 0.282 / 0.342 off it. The route is inside the noise band of the non-route. The floor does not know where people walk.
F2.Q10:
There are two openings: the south corridor mouth at x 370–445, y≈265, and the room continuing north off the top of the frame across its full width (that's the camera edge, not a doorway — the east wall at x≈630 and the west wall at x≈180 are solid).

Judged on the ground in front of them, **they look the same.** The apron in front of the south mouth (372–446, 225–264) measures 0.334 dark-mark coverage; the north strip (192–608, 8–40) measures within the same band. No threshold, no darkening, no polish, no scatter differential, no directional smear at either. If one of these is the door four hundred years of orc-soldiers use and the other is sealed, the floor does not say which.
F2.CULL: Slab faces are blank at 1:1; joints, cracks and stains share one value and collapse into a single black web.
F2.FLIP LIST:
- Separate the three dark elements by value: keep mortar joints mid-tone (around `140,105,70`), push cracks darker and thinner than joints, and give stains a colour cast so they don't read as holes — right now (347,175), (303,206) and (268,232) are all within 20 levels.
- Put wear on the route: darken and smooth a 2-slab-wide tread band through the doorway at (372–446, 225–264) and down the corridor centre, with grit and unwalked texture surviving at the corridor edges. The player should be able to find the exit with the lamp alone.
- Get legible texture onto the faces at 1:1 — pitting, scattered dark aggregate specks, uneven fill — and clamp the lamp's highlight so it stops clipping to `255` across (289–426, 87–254) and bleaching the slabs under the figure.
- Break the 0/45/90 lock: cracks and stain silhouettes need mark angles off the four cardinals, and slab edges need chipping and rounding so corners aren't all clean 90° pixels.
- Cut the rosette count by half and cluster what remains — pooled at a wall base, trailing from one point — instead of one every ~3 tiles at uniform density across the whole room.

---

Worth flagging beyond the questions: the biggest single hit to this floor isn't drawn at all. The stair-stepped light seam through (330,60)→(200,190) and the highlight clipping under the lamp are lighting-pipeline problems, and they're currently louder than every mark the floor artist made. Fixing the art without fixing the light band will not change what a player sees.

F1.Q1: Dry-laid cut stone paving — rectangular ashlar slabs, pale sandstone/limestone colour, set in a recessed dark joint grid.
F1.Q1_WHY:
Slabs sit on a 32px grid with horizontal joints landing at y≡15–18 mod 32 (measured, not guessed), in a staggered bond with mixed widths — singles and doubles. The joints are a consistent 3–4px band, darker than the slab and recessed, which reads as a mortarless butt joint packed with dirt. What tells me it's stone and not anything else is negative evidence: no grain, no plank ends, no tile repeat, no brick module. What I can't tell you is *what* stone. The faces at (270–420, 100–270) are a single flat value. There is no aggregate, no bedding plane, no colour variation within a slab, no tonal difference between one slab and its neighbour. It is stone-shaped, not stone-surfaced.

---
F1.Q2:
South, down the corridor at x 370–440.

**Nothing about the ground influenced that.** I read it entirely off the walls — the placeholder blocks pinch to a channel and that's the only gap in the south side. I checked the ground in front of it first: the corridor mouth at (370–440, 250–300) is indistinguishable from the middle of the room. Same slab sizes, same blank faces, same joint darkness. If I deleted the walls from this image I would have no reason to walk south rather than north, east or west.

---
F1.Q3: It has been cracked, and that is the entire event history. A network of thin fractures runs through the chamber. Beyond that the floor is in delivery condition.
F1.Q3_WHY:
What I looked for and did not find, by region:

- **No traffic.** The corridor at (355–445, 270–520), brightened 2.2×, is completely bare — not one mark, chip or scuff over roughly 40 slab faces on the one route the figure must take.
- **No wear differential.** The centre of the chamber and the corners are the same. No polish, no dishing, no lightened track.
- **No dirt.** Joints are the same value everywhere; nothing has drifted into a corner or banked against a wall.
- **No damage other than cracks.** Slab corners at (470–630, 60–250) are all square. Nothing spalled, nothing lipped, nothing sunk out of plane.
- **No repair.** This is the floor of a place held by a company that patches everything with rope, pins and salvaged timber for four hundred years. There is not one driven pin, one packed shim, one board over a hole, anywhere on the walkable ground.

The cracks themselves don't behave like damage. Magnified 7× at (200–320, 90–180), the crack running down x≈257 passes straight through the horizontal joints at y≈115 and y≈147 — no deflection, no widening at the joint, and it resumes in near-perfect alignment on the far slab. Stone fractures divert into joints; this one ignores them. It's a polyline drawn over the finished tilemap.

---
F1.Q4:
Two things.

1. **The cracks read as unlit ink.** I sampled crack pixels against their surrounding slab: at (257,140) the crack is value 22 against a slab at 139; at (600,160) the crack is 36 against a slab at 36. The crack sits at a fixed near-black across the entire lighting range while the stone under it swings by 100+ levels. In the lit core it is therefore the highest-contrast thing on screen — higher than the joints, higher than anything on the figure's own sprite — and my eye goes to it every time instead of to the lamp or the exit.

2. **The diagonal hatch motif.** Groups of parallel 45° scratch lines recur across the dim band at (470–660, 60–250) and again along the top at (190–470, 0–55) — same angle, same spacing, same 1px weight, on slab after slab. Six or seven instances within the crop at (470–660, 60–250) alone. It stops being marks on stone and becomes one texture stamped repeatedly.

---
F1.Q5:
**Made.** I tested it rather than eyeballing it: high-passed the image to strip the lighting, masked out the joint pixels, and correlated all 98 floor tile faces pairwise. Median correlation 0.118. The handful of matches above 0.85 — (212,83) vs (276,115) vs (468,115) — turned out on inspection to be *blank* faces matching each other on their shared joint edge, not repeated texture. The masonry layout is genuinely authored: varied widths, real staggering, no tiling period.

The caveat matters though. What was made here is the *layout*. The layout is then faced with a surface that wasn't made at all — flat fill. So it passes the repetition test by having nothing to repeat.

---
F1.Q6:
**YES.**

Merely competent. The lighting is handsome, the masonry layout is well varied, and it would not embarrass anyone on a store page. It is not genuinely good. Genuinely good floor art tells you where you are and what has happened there; this tells you neither, and its strongest visual element — the cracks — is a rendering bug.

---
F1.Q7:
**Legible at 1:1:** the joint grid, the slab layout, the crack lines, the lamp gradient, and one soft diagonal light streak running roughly (420,20) → (200,270). Every one of those is layout or lighting. **On the faces themselves, at 1:1, in the lit core: nothing.** They are blank.

**Only appears once magnified:** the diagonal hatch groups and the short horizontal dash stacks. And "magnified" undersells it — 4× alone wasn't enough on the dim band; I had to magnify *and* brighten 2.6× before those marks resolved into anything I could name.

**The middle case, stated honestly:** in the dim band at 1:1 there is a scratchy something on the faces. I can see that the faces aren't empty. I cannot tell you what any of it is. That is texture as noise, not texture as information.

**The measurement:** counting non-joint pixels that sit between 66% and 93% of their local brightness — i.e. actual marks on a face — gives **0.6% of face area in the lit core (270–420, 100–270)** against **13.9% in the dim right band (470–660, 60–250)**. Nothing is clipped in the core; zero pixels reach 250. The detail isn't blown out. It was never drawn there.
F1.Q7_WHY:
- *Checked at 1:1:* (260–420, 60–270) lit core — blank faces. (200–440, 180–300) lower lit — blank faces, two crack lines. (440–680, 60–240) dim right — scratchy noise, unresolvable. (355–445, 270–520) corridor — blank.
- *Had to magnify:* (470–660, 60–250) at 5× **and** +2.6 brightness to resolve hatch groups and dash stacks. (200–320, 90–180) at 7× to establish the crack/joint behaviour. (355–445, 270–520) at 6× **and** +2.2 brightness to confirm the corridor is empty rather than merely dark.

---
F1.Q8:
It reads as **two ages that contradict each other**, and the contradiction is the answer.

**Under the lamp — (270–420, 100–270) — it reads as laid last year.** Square corners, faces flat and unmarked, joints uniform, no dishing, no dirt. Then someone drew century-old fractures across it. That's the conflict: the cracks assert great age and the surface they're drawn on refuses to corroborate it. The cracks lose, because they're the thing that reads as ink.

**In the dim band — (470–660, 60–250) and (190–470, 0–55) — it reads older**, maybe a few centuries: the faces are covered in marks. But I only know that because I brightened the image. At the size the game is played, that age is not communicated.

So: the parts you can see read new, and the parts that read old you can't see. Nowhere on this floor does it read as older than the records — nothing here has been in continuous heavy use for an unrecorded span. Heavy use leaves a shape, and this floor has no shape.

---
F1.Q9: **No. The ground told me nothing.** I read the corridor off the walls.
F1.Q9_WHY:
- *Route I'd take:* south through (370–440, 250–300), then (370–440, 300–430), which is still inside useful light — the slab faces there hold value 66–100, well above black.
- *Regions I rejected:* north across (220–620, 0–60); east toward (560–630, 100–250); west toward (185–260, 100–250). All within the lamp.
- *What is different about the ground between them:* **nothing.** Same slab module, same joint value, same blank faces, same absence of dirt or polish. I ran the mark-density measure on the corridor thinking I'd found something at 9.7% — magnifying and brightening it showed that number was the lamp falloff gradient, not marks. The corridor floor is bare.

A route walked daily should be the easiest thing in this image to read, and it is invisible. If I turned the walls off, the ground would leave me standing still.

---
F1.Q10:
**They all look the same.** There are two openings: the south corridor mouth at (370–440, 250–275) and the north continuation across the full top edge (220–620, 0–15). The ground immediately in front of each is identical — same slab sizes, same blank faces, same joint darkness, no dirt tracked in from either, no threshold wear, no fan of scuffing spreading from either mouth into the room. A door nobody has opened in three hundred years and a door a company marches through daily are, on this floor, the same door.

---
F1.CULL:
Under the lamp the slab faces are blank; the only detail is unlit cracks drawn over the joints.

---
F1.FLIP LIST:
- Put legible material on the faces inside the lamp's bright core (270–420, 100–270) — pitting, chipped arrises, colour variation slab-to-slab — at a contrast that survives at 1:1 without magnifying.
- Light the cracks with the scene: multiply them into the slab rather than compositing at fixed near-black, so they stop out-contrasting everything at (257,110–180) and fade with the falloff like the stone does.
- Break the cracks at the joints — deflect them into the joint line or terminate them there, and vary width and value along the run instead of a uniform 1px.
- Wear the route: darken and smooth the slabs along (370–440, 250–520) and fan that wear into the chamber from both openings, so the corridor and the north edge stop reading identically to a dead corner.
- Add the garrison's repairs to the walkable ground — driven pins, packed shims, a salvaged board over a broken slab — at least three instances inside the lit chamber.

---

Nothing here is unrecoverable. The layout work and the lighting are the expensive parts and both are already done well; what's missing is the material pass on the slab faces and one blend-mode fix on the crack overlay. The floor's real problem isn't quality, it's that it carries no information — a player standing on it learns nothing about where to go or what this place has been through, which for a dungeon floor is the whole job.
